Churl
chûrl
n. (a niggardly man; one whose instruments are evil, set opposite the liberal)
Old English ceorl, a common freeman, then by long descent a rude and grasping man. The Hebrew kilay in Isaiah 32 means the crafty, the miserly, the man who deals by fraud.

Biblical Definition

Isaiah 32 describes the kingdom of the righteous King, and one mark of it is that words go back to meaning what they mean: “The vile person shall be no more called liberal, nor the churl said to be bountiful” (Isa 32:5). Two lies are broken in one verse. Under the old order the vile man was flattered as generous and the churl was praised as bountiful, because whoever holds the purse also holds the vocabulary. The prophet then shows the churl at work: “The instruments also of the churl are evil: he deviseth wicked devices to destroy the poor with lying words, even when the needy speaketh right” (Isa 32:7). He is not merely tight-fisted. He has instruments — means, contrivances, a method — and the method is lying words used against a poor man whose case is honest. Set against him stands one sentence of quiet greatness: “But the liberal deviseth liberal things; and by liberal things shall he stand” (Isa 32:8). Both men devise. The difference is what they devise and what they stand on at the last. Proverbs adds the promise that governs a bountiful hand: “The liberal soul shall be made fat: and he that watereth shall be watered also himself” (Pro 11:25). The churl keeps and shrinks; the liberal pours and stands.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a churl as a rustic or countryman, then a rude, surly, ill-bred man, and particularly a niggard or miser — one of a close and grasping disposition.

expand to see more

CHURL, n. [Sax. ceorl, a man, a freeman of the lowest rank.] A rustic; a countryman or labourer.

2. A rude, surly, ill-bred man.

3. A miser; a niggard; a man of a close and grasping disposition.

The churl said to be bountiful. Isa. xxxii.

Key Scripture

Isa 32:5 — "The vile person shall be no more called liberal, nor the churl said to be bountiful."

Isa 32:7 — "The instruments also of the churl are evil: he deviseth wicked devices to destroy the poor with lying words, even when the needy speaketh right."

Isa 32:8 — "But the liberal deviseth liberal things; and by liberal things shall he stand."

Pro 11:25 — "The liberal soul shall be made fat: and he that watereth shall be watered also himself."

Modern Corruption

The churl's oldest trick is not hoarding but renaming, and Isaiah 32:5 promises a kingdom in which the flattering name is taken away from him.

expand to see more

The verse names a corruption of language before it names a corruption of money. A vile man was called liberal; a churl was said to be bountiful. The lie was not told by the churl alone but by the men around him who needed his favour, and it worked because generosity is measured by reputation rather than by what actually reaches the poor. Every age repeats it. A man whose gains are wrung out of the needy endows a wing that carries his name and is thanked publicly for his bounty; the announcement is the gift, and the poor whose case was crushed with lying words are no better fed. Isaiah's promise is that the righteous King restores the plain meaning of words, and that restoration is itself a mercy to the poor, because a man who can no longer buy the name of generous must either become generous or be known.

There is a churlishness that never touches money at all, and Scripture is as severe with it. The churl of Isaiah 32:7 destroys the poor with lying words — his instrument is speech, and his victim is a man whose case is right. That is the churl in the assembly, in the court, in the eldership: the one who cannot be generous with a brother's reputation, who devises a construction of his neighbour's words that no honest hearing would allow. Against him the eighth verse sets the only stability there is. The liberal man stands — not because giving purchases anything, for grace is not bought, but because a bountiful hand is the fruit of a heart that has received freely and therefore has nothing to protect. Nabal, whose very name means folly, is the churl of the histories, and his end is the commentary on this proverb.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew kilay (H3596), the crafty, churlish, miserly man; contrasted with nadiyb (H5081), the noble, willing, liberal man; both in Isaiah 32.

expand to see more

Hebrew kilay (H3596) — a churl, a knave; the miser whose dealings are fraud; Isaiah 32:5, Isaiah 32:7.

Hebrew nadiyb (H5081) — noble, willing, liberal; the opposite man of the same passage, whose devices are liberal things; Isaiah 32:8.

Hebrew ebyown (H34) — the needy, the man in want who here speaks right and is answered with lying words; Isaiah 32:7.

Hebrew nabal (H5036) — foolish, vile; the root behind the name of the churl of Carmel who railed on David's young men; 1 Samuel 25:25.

Greek pleonexia (G4124) — covetousness, the grasping temper the New Testament names as idolatry; Colossians 3:5.

Usage

"“Nor the churl said to be bountiful” — the flattering name taken away in the King's kingdom."

"“The instruments also of the churl are evil” — his weapon is lying words against an honest case."

"“By liberal things shall he stand” — the open hand is the standing one."
